greeting: Happy Friday, Bay View, and yes, it's Friday the 13th. Expect a gray, breezy morning with a chance of a shower before the sun takes over for a dry, mostly sunny weekend. Today we've got the MPS budget picture, a neighborhood fish fry roundup and a 70-year-old Serbian landmark in the spotlight.

top.title: MPS chief: a $58 million deficit and fewer students than expected
top.dek: In her first State of Our Schools speech, Cassellius said the district's budget gap has grown as enrollment slipped.
top.body:
Milwaukee Public Schools Superintendent Brenda Cassellius used her first State of Our Schools address on Thursday at Discovery World to lay out a tough budget picture, under the theme "stability first, excellence next."

According to WPR, the district's deficit has grown to about $58 million, up from the $46 million gap the board tried to close with cuts in February. Enrollment came in at 58,088 students, about 2,200 below projections, which means less state aid.

WISN reported that she offered no timeline for another referendum. She pointed to roughly 300 central-office jobs cut, a small gain in grade 3-8 reading scores on the Forward Exam (23.6% to 25.1%) and a drop in student gun deaths from 23 to 12. State report cards are due next week, and the board is nearing a vote on a long-range facilities plan that would close and merge several schools, which matters for every MPS family in Bay View.

image.alt: A Milwaukee Public Schools entrance sign on a school building

top.title: The gas station owner on Bay View's southern edge who knows customers by name
top.dek: WUWM profiles Faisal Bhimani, whose two stations at Howard and Clement double as a neighborhood hub.
top.body:
WUWM spent time with Faisal Bhimani, who owns the BP and Citgo stations facing each other at Howard and Clement avenues, just south of Bay View on the St. Francis side.

Bhimani hands out free food and drinks, lets local groups hold fundraisers on his lot and has given free gas to seniors living on tight budgets. A lemonade-stand tradition he started has outlasted the kids who first ran it; they're in college now.

He told the station that neighbors kept him afloat during the Howard Avenue reconstruction by using the one entrance left open. On Bay View Town Hall, Bhimani thanked Bay View and St. Francis for the support.

image.alt: Faisal Bhimani behind the counter of his gas station

top.title: Aerial Hippie brings circus-style fitness to the Hide House
top.dek: WISN visited the Bay View studio where beginners learn to climb and spin on hanging fabric.
top.body:
WISN 12's In Your Neighborhood segment stopped by Aerial Hippie, an aerial fitness studio at 2625 S. Greeley St., near Greeley and Dover.

Classes use hanging fabric slings and are inspired by circus silks. Instructor Beth Stavros told the station the classes are open to every skill level, and beginner sessions run on Saturday mornings and early afternoons.

Details and class sign-ups are on the studio's website, aerialhippiemke.com.

image.alt: Students practicing on hanging fabric slings at Aerial Hippie

schools.title: MPS rebids the Lincoln Avenue School demolition a third time
schools.dek: After a bidder objected, the fire-damaged school's demolition will now go to the lowest qualified bid.
schools.body:
Milwaukee Public Schools threw out the bids to tear down the fire-damaged Lincoln Avenue Elementary, 1817 W. Lincoln Ave., and will re-advertise the job as a sealed competitive bid that goes to the lowest responsive, responsible bidder.

Urban Milwaukee reports the switch followed an objection from West Milwaukee-based The MRD Group, which bid about $928,000; the district had chosen an Illinois firm at about $4.8 million.

The school sits west of Bay View, but the episode is part of a broader look at MPS spending: FOX6 also raised questions this week about the district's finance office.

image.alt: Aerial view of the fire-damaged Lincoln Avenue School and surrounding blocks

parks.title: Restored Vietnam Veterans Memorial rededicated on the lakefront
parks.dek: About 100 Vietnam veterans gathered in Veterans Park for the unveiling of a $1 million restoration.
parks.body:
The Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Veterans Park, on the lakefront north of downtown, was rededicated on Veterans Day after a $1 million restoration.

Urban Milwaukee reports that about 100 Vietnam veterans attended. Speakers included Maj. Gen. Brian Winski of the War Memorial Center, Gov.-elect David Crowley and Mayor Cavalier Johnson.

image.alt: Veterans gathered in front of the restored Vietnam Veterans Memorial's three steel pillars

fishfry.title: Friday fish fry: where to find one in Bay View tonight
fishfry.dek: Beer-battered cod on Howell, Dutch-style haddock on KK, Vietnamese swai and a Conway Street classic.
fishfry.body:
It's Friday in Wisconsin, so here's where Bay View fries fish. Heirloom MKE (2378 S. Howell Ave.) does Fish Fry Friday from 4 to 9 p.m.: two pieces of beer-battered cod with fries, coleslaw, tartar, buttered rye and lemon. Reservations are recommended.

Centraal Grand Cafe & Tappery (2306 S. Kinnickinnic Ave.) serves a Fridays-only crispy haddock fry with coleslaw, tartar, friets and rye, starting at 11 a.m. Hue (2699 S. Kinnickinnic Ave.) puts a Vietnamese spin on it after 4 p.m., with beer-battered swai, garlic fried rice and Asian slaw.

Dom & Phil DeMarinis (1211 E. Conway St.) lists a $14 Friday beer-batter cod fry with fries, potato pancakes or pasta, plus salad and bread. Check each spot's hours before heading out, and tell us your favorite through the tip form.

image.alt: The front entrance of Heirloom MKE on S. Howell Ave.

pets.title: Cat of the Week: Skeeter wants to go home with a sibling
pets.dek: A playful orange tabby, born in April, is up for adoption along with his littermates.
pets.body:
Milwaukee Record and Urban Cat Coalition's Cat of the Week is Skeeter, an orange tabby born in April. He's neutered, vaccinated and house-trained, and gets along with kids and other cats.

The catch: he has to be adopted with at least one of his siblings, Zinnia, Mango or Frodo. Details and the adoption application are at the link.

spotlight.title: Spotlight: Three Brothers
spotlight.dek: Seventy years in an old Schlitz tavern: Bay View's Serbian landmark still makes burek the way Mama did.
spotlight.body:
On a quiet residential corner of Bay View, Three Brothers has served Serbian home cooking at 2414 S. St. Clair St. since 1956, which makes 2026 its 70th year. The cream city brick building went up around the turn of the last century as a Schlitz tied house, and the brewery's belted globe still crowns its turret. Much of that era survives inside: the original bar, a Grand Tetons mural behind it, bentwood chairs and Formica-topped tables.

Founder Milun Radicevic, a Serbian army veteran who survived imprisonment during World War II, came to Milwaukee in 1949 and ran a tavern on S. 2nd Street before buying this building. He named the restaurant for his three sons, who were still in Yugoslavia at the time, and his wife, Milunka, built the menu from her own recipes. Their son Branko later left a banking career in California to help when his father fell ill, and Branko's wife, Patricia, learned the recipes at her mother-in-law's side and took over the kitchen in 1982. Branko died in 2015. Patricia and her children carry it on today, and only family members have ever done the cooking.

The menu has barely changed in decades. The star is burek, flaky layers of paper-thin filo filled with beef, cheese, or spinach and cheese; it takes a while to bake, so regulars call ahead to order it. Other staples include sarma (stuffed cabbage), chicken paprikash, goulash with potato dumplings, chevapchichi sausages, raznjici pork skewers, roast lamb, duck and even goose, with house-made desserts like strudel, baklava and a seven-layer walnut torte. Given a day and a half's notice, the kitchen can adapt dishes for vegetarian, vegan or gluten-free diners.

The accolades go back a long way. The James Beard Foundation named Three Brothers an America's Classic in 2002, and the city designated the building a Milwaukee landmark in 1976. The restaurant has turned up in Gourmet, Bon Appétit and The New York Times, and in 2025 USA Today put it on its national Restaurants of the Year list.

If you go, plan ahead: reservations are recommended, and the restaurant takes cash or checks only (there's an ATM next door at DeMarinis). With holiday gatherings coming up, it's worth calling early if you have your heart set on burek or a roast.

Three Brothers, 2414 S. St. Clair St. Open Wednesday to Friday 5 to 9 p.m. and Saturday and Sunday 4 to 9 p.m.; closed Monday and Tuesday. Call (414) 481-7530, visit threebrothersmke.com or follow @threebrothersmke on Instagram.

history.text: Bay View governed itself as a village for eight years before its roughly 4,000 residents voted in 1887 to join Milwaukee, becoming the city's 17th Ward. The trade gave up independence for city services residents wanted, such as sewers, sidewalks and street lights. The Beulah Brinton House, pictured, was an early gathering place for the village and is now home to the Bay View Historical Society.

buzz.headline: Did your city bill just jump? Neighbors say theirs did
buzz.body: A post asking whether anyone else's city water bill shot up drew more than 100 comments, with several neighbors saying theirs ran about $50 higher than usual. Some pointed to the once-a-year snow and ice charge, though at least one said the jump showed up even without it. We didn't find a new rate hike announced this fall; the city's posted 2026 charges list the snow and ice fee at $1.19 per foot of street frontage, billed once a year, plus a quarterly solid waste charge of $67.95.

buzz.headline: Metal detector turns up old silver in a Bay View yard
buzz.body: A neighbor shared a haul from a metal-detecting session at a Bay View house, and the group was charmed. Commenters swooned over the clink of old silver quarters, and one recognized an old toy cap dart from childhood.

buzz.headline: A 600-foot freighter is waiting off the harbor
buzz.body: A Reddit photo of the cargo ship Verila, anchored off Milwaukee's harbor at sunrise, had people asking why. The poster's take: ships sometimes wait offshore rather than pay to tie up at the dock. If you've seen a big ship sitting still off South Shore, that's likely the one.
